title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Map and question the scholarly discourse around a topic, starting from wherever you are.

title: Starting from a textbook is not a weakness
body: It is tempting to think that a 'proper' discourse map has to start with journal articles. It does not. Starting from a textbook, as a less experienced reader, is a sensible first step, provided you then use it to open up the wider discourse rather than stopping there.

title: The book's own example
body: Dennis and Abbott (2026, pp.118-119) illustrate this with a worked example. 'As a less experienced learner, and with the principle of ‘building knowledge’ in mind, John begins by looking at the textbook he found, Creativity in Primary Education, edited by Anthony Wilson (3rd ed., 2015).' John's starting point is ordinary. What matters is what he does with it next: using it to find the wider positions in the field, not treating it as the final word.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students who have each gathered a small set of sources on the same topic.

{{learner-a}} finds three sources on a topic and lists them in the essay, one after another, with no sense of how they relate.

{{learner-b}} finds the same three sources, but groups them by the position each one takes, and writes one question against each group: what is this group assuming, and who does its claim affect?

Both had the sources. Only {{learner-b}} had mapped the discourse, rather than just listing it.

title: Why grouping and tagging counts as mapping
body: A list of sources is not a map. A map groups positions together and asks a question of each group. That is what turns 'I found some sources' into 'I have mapped and questioned the discourse around this topic', which is the skill this lesson is building.

displayTitle: Three ways to start opening up a discourse
body: Different starting points all lead to the same destination: a mapped, questioned discourse.
instruction: Select each tab to see how that starting point leads on to mapping the wider discourse.

_items.title: From a textbook
_items.body: A textbook gives you the settled, well-established version of a topic. Use its references and signposting to find the live debates it is built on, then go looking for the positions on either side.

_items.title: From a review article
_items.body: A review article has already grouped positions for you. Use its groupings as a starting map, then check whether more recent work has shifted the picture it describes.

_items.title: From a recent journal paper
_items.body: A recent paper usually opens by placing itself against existing positions. Use its own framing of the debate as a starting map, then check who it has left out.

instruction: Select a highlighted phrase to see why it matters.

_passage.text: Three positions on this topic can be grouped as follows:
Group A argues the effect is strong
_passage._note: Naming the position, not just the authors, is what makes this a map rather than a list.

_passage.text: Group B argues it is weak once other factors are controlled for
_passage._note: A genuine discourse map needs the disagreement stated, not smoothed over.

_passage.text: Group C questions whether the effect can be measured at all
_passage._note: The question a group leaves open is often more useful than its headline claim.

title: Building your own map
body: Start wherever you are, even a textbook. List the positions you find, group them, and write one question against each group: what is it assuming, and who does it affect. That one-page map is the mapping and questioning this lesson is about.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Pick a topic from your own course. What is the first, most accessible source you would start from?
What question would you ask of the position that source takes?
